doc.title: Types
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script can annotate variables, function parameters and returns, and local type names with Adaptive data types and simple structured types. Leaves are registered data types such as integer, string, boolean, object, array, any, and void.

These annotations are part of the script language. They are separate from adaptive object types and property meta used by adapters and requests. Object-type rules at the adapter and request layer are unchanged. Script type and interface declarations define shapes used only for script type checking.
Railroad diagrams below match the harvested grammar productions. For the complete syntax, see the .

section.title: Type
section.paragraph: A Type is a union of intersection types (see below). That is the top production used wherever a type is written: after : on bindings and parameters, in type aliases, and in object and function type forms.
Older spellings such as (array of integer) or (object "…") are not accepted.

section.title: Example
TypeName and DataType
section.paragraph: A primary type is a type name, an object type literal, a tuple, a parenthesized or function type, or Array<Type>. A type name is either an Adaptive data type id or a name declared with type / interface in the script.

section.title: Example
ArrayType
section.paragraph: Write an array of element type T as T[], or as Array<T> (same meaning). Multiple [] suffixes nest (for example integer[][]).

section.title: Example
TupleType
section.paragraph: A tuple type lists element types in order inside [ … ]. Length and each position matter when the value is known (for example a list literal).

section.title: IntersectionType
section.paragraph: An intersection type is one or more array types joined with &. A value must satisfy every arm.

section.title: Example
UnionType
section.paragraph: A union type is one or more intersection types joined with |. A value may match any arm.

section.title: Example
section.code: const u: integer | string = 1; const v: integer | string | boolean = true;

section.title: ObjectTypeLiteral
section.paragraph: An object type literal lists named properties with types. A trailing ? after a property name marks it optional. Property names may be identifiers or string literals.
This is a script shape only. It does not import an adaptive object type from an adapter catalog.

section.title: Example
section.code: const o: { host: string, port?: integer } = { host: "h" };

section.title: FunctionType
section.paragraph: A function type describes a callable value: (parameters) => Return. Parameters may be named with optional ? and rest ..., or written as bare type names. A parenthesized type that is not a function type is still a parenthesized Type.
Script function values use function (…): Return (colon before the return type). That is the value form; the type annotation form uses =>.

section.title: Example
OptionalType and OptionalReturnType
section.paragraph: An optional type is a leading : and a Type. That form appears on const / let bindings, pattern leaves, parameters, and similar places. Optional return type is the same idea on a script function declaration.

section.title: Example
Type statement
section.paragraph: type Name = Type; declares a local alias for a type. The name may then be used as a type name in the same script unit.

section.title: Example
section.code: type Id = integer; const x: Id = 3;

section.title: Interface statement
section.paragraph: interface declares a named object shape. Use extends for one or more base interfaces. Optional properties use ? after the property name.

section.title: Example
Type checking (default off)
section.paragraph: Type annotations are always accepted by the compiler. Checking is off by default so existing scripts keep working. Turn checking on with environment flags when you want mismatches reported.

list.item: compile:typeCheck — checks at compile time when the right-hand side type is known, and at runtime on assignment and script function parameters.
compile:typeCheckCompileOnly — compile-time checks only (used instead of full typeCheck when both are set).
compile:noImplicitAny — when checking is active, a missing annotation is an error instead of any.
compile:strictNullChecks — stricter handling of null and undefined.
compile:strict — turns on typeCheck, noImplicitAny, and strictNullChecks together.

section.paragraph: Flags may be set from the host environment or with flag_set in a script. When compile checking is on, calls to known Adaptive functions are also checked at compile time against each function’s parameter and return data types (when those types can be determined without running the call).

section.title: What is checked

list.item: Data type leaves (for example integer versus string).
Array types: the value must be an array; element types are checked when the value is known (for example an array literal).
Tuples: length and each position when the value is known.

Object and interface shapes: required properties must be present; property values must match their types; extends bases are included. An object literal may not include properties outside the type (including when used as a function argument). Object literals with spreads or computed property names skip that extra-key check. At runtime, values that are not object literals may still have extra properties, so adaptive objects can be wider than the script type.
Function return types when a return type is declared.
Function types: script functions and closures are checked for parameter and return compatibility; other function values only need data type function.
Array and object patterns: binding annotations such as const [a: integer] = … or { host: h: string } are enforced when checking is on.

section.paragraph: Bindings without an annotation, and data that arrives from outside the script, are treated as any at compile time unless noImplicitAny is set. Runtime data type and adaptive object-type rules still apply on their own.
